idiom_name: hand-written attempt loop over clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) with a rand_r jitter draw
implementation_notes: C has no retry primitive and no schedule type, so the pattern is entirely hand-written: try the call, classify the error code, compute min(cap, base * multiplier^(attempt-1)), draw the jitter, wait, try again. The wait must use clock_nanosleep against CLOCK_MONOTONIC (nanosleep measures against CLOCK_REALTIME, which a clock adjustment can move) and must handle EINTR by re-entering the sleep with the remaining timespec, because clock_nanosleep is never restarted automatically. Keep the attempt count and the elapsed budget in the call's own state, and draw jitter from a caller-owned seed (rand_r) rather than shared global rand(), which is neither thread-safe nor per-call reproducible. The network-level ancestor of this pattern, TCP backoff, is standardized in RFC 6298, where the RTO doubles on every retransmission and may be capped - the caller-side version needs the same cap plus jitter.
pitfalls: sleep() only resolves whole seconds and nanosleep() measures against CLOCK_REALTIME, so a wall-clock adjustment can stretch or shorten the delay; use clock_nanosleep with CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
clock_nanosleep is never restarted after a signal; ignoring EINTR cuts the wait short and the next attempt arrives early.
A for(;;) loop with an attempt counter but no deadline is a hot loop the moment the failure is permanent, and global rand() is not thread-safe - use rand_r or a caller-supplied generator.
